title: Probability
description: The probability scale, calculating simple probabilities, sample spaces, and experimental vs theoretical probability.

notes.heading: The Probability Scale
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that tells us how likely an event is to happen. It can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percentage.

🔑 Key Concept
The probability scale runs from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A probability of 0.5 means an event is equally likely to happen as not.

💡 Worked Example
A weather forecast says there is a 75% chance of rain.
• As a decimal: 0.75
• As a fraction: $\dfrac{75}{100}=\dfrac{3}{4}$
• On the probability scale: close to certain, but not guaranteed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• 0 = impossible
• 1 = certain
• 0.5 = even chance
• Probabilities can be written as fractions, decimals or percentages
• Every probability must lie between 0 and 1

⚠️ Common Misconception
A high probability such as 0.9 does not mean an event will definitely happen; it means the event is very likely. Only $P=1$ is certain.

notes.heading: Calculating Simple Probability
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The theoretical probability of an event is calculated as:
$$P(\text{event})=\dfrac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{total number of possible outcomes}}$$

🔑 Key Concept
Favourable outcomes are the ones we want. The total must include every possible result, and every result must be equally likely.

💡 Worked Example
A bag contains 4 red, 5 blue and 6 green marbles. What is the probability of choosing a red marble?

Step 1: Find the total number of marbles.
$$4+5+6=15$$

Step 2: Identify the number of favourable outcomes.
There are 4 red marbles.

Step 3: Write the probability.
$$P(\text{red})=\dfrac{4}{15}$$

✅ Check
The fraction is already in its simplest form and $\dfrac{4}{15}$ is between 0 and 1. ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always count the total carefully
• Simplify fractions when possible
• Probabilities must be between 0 and 1
• The sum of the probabilities of all possible outcomes equals 1

notes.heading: Complementary Events
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The complement of an event $A$ is the event that $A$ does NOT happen. We write it as $P(\text{not }A)$ or $P(A\prime)$.

🔑 Key Concept
Because an event either happens or it does not:
$$P(A)+P(\text{not }A)=1$$
So:
$$P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$$

💡 Worked Example
The probability that it rains tomorrow is 0.3. What is the probability it does not rain?

Step 1: Use the complement rule.
$$P(\text{not rain})=1-P(\text{rain})$$

Step 2: Substitute.
$$P(\text{not rain})=1-0.3=0.7$$

✅ Tip
Using complements is often quicker than counting all the outcomes you do not want.

notes.heading: Sample Spaces and Listing Outcomes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment.

🔑 Key Concept
Listing outcomes carefully helps us count the total and find probabilities. For two experiments, use a table or a tree diagram so you do not miss any possibilities.

💡 Worked Example
Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. Use a sample-space table to find $P(\text{total }=7)$.

Step 1: There are $6\times 6=36$ equally likely outcomes.

Step 2: List the pairs that give a total of 7:
$$(1,6),\,(2,5),\,(3,4),\,(4,3),\,(5,2),\,(6,1)$$
There are 6 favourable outcomes.

Step 3: Calculate the probability.
$$P(\text{total }=7)=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac{1}{6}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 'a total of 7' as a single outcome. It is actually made up of several different equally likely outcomes.

notes.heading: Experimental and Theoretical Probability
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Theoretical probability is what should happen, calculated from the sample space. Experimental probability, also called relative frequency, is what actually happened in an experiment.

🔑 Key Concept
$$\text{relative frequency}=\dfrac{\text{number of times the event happened}}{\text{total number of trials}}$$

💡 Worked Example
A coin is flipped 80 times and lands on heads 34 times.

Theoretical probability of heads:
$$P(\text{heads})=\dfrac{1}{2}=0.5$$

Experimental probability of heads:
$$\text{relative frequency}=\dfrac{34}{80}=\dfrac{17}{40}=0.425$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Experimental probability changes with each set of trials
• More trials usually make the experimental probability closer to the theoretical probability
• This pattern is called the law of large numbers
• A single coin flip is still theoretical $P=0.5$; the actual result is either heads or tails

notes.heading: Equally Likely Outcomes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Outcomes are equally likely when each one has the same chance of happening.

🔑 Key Concept
The formula $P=\dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}$ only works when all outcomes are equally likely. If a spinner has a larger red section, red is more likely than blue.

💡 Worked Example
A spinner is divided into 8 equal sectors: 3 red, 3 blue and 2 green. What is $P(\text{red})$?

Because the sectors are equal:
$$P(\text{red})=\dfrac{3}{8}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the number of colours as the total. There are 3 colours, but they are not equally likely because red and blue each have 3 sectors while green has 2.

✅ Tip
Before calculating, ask: 'Is every outcome fair?' If not, you cannot use the simple fraction formula.

notes.heading: Solving Probability Problems
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A probability problem may ask you to combine several ideas: sample spaces, complements, fractions and checking your answer.

🔑 How it works
Step 1: Identify the experiment and list all possible outcomes.
Step 2: Count the favourable outcomes.
Step 3: Use $P=\dfrac{\text{favourable}}{\text{total}}$.
Step 4: Simplify and check the answer makes sense.

💡 Worked Example
A letter is chosen at random from the word PROBABILITY. What is the probability of choosing a vowel?

Step 1: Count total letters.
The word has 11 letters.

Step 2: Count vowels.
O, A, I, I = 4 vowels.

Step 3: Write the probability.
$$P(\text{vowel})=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

✅ Check
The answer $\dfrac{4}{11}$ is between 0 and 1, and the fraction is already in its simplest form.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Read the question carefully to identify what is being chosen
• Repeated letters count separately
• Always check that the probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1

flashcards.definition: A number from 0 to 1 that measures how likely an event is to happen.
A single possible result of an experiment.
flashcards.example: When rolling a die, landing on 3 is one outcome.

flashcards.definition: A set of one or more outcomes that we are interested in.
flashcards.example: Rolling an even number on a die is the event {2, 4, 6}.

flashcards.definition: The list of all possible outcomes of an experiment.
flashcards.example: For a fair die the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

flashcards.definition: An outcome that makes the event happen.
flashcards.example: For the event "roll a number greater than 4", the favourable outcomes are 5 and 6.

flashcards.definition: Probability calculated using the sample space when all outcomes are equally likely.
Probability based on the results of an experiment; also called relative frequency.
Every outcome has the same chance of happening.
flashcards.example: A fair six-sided die has $P(\text{rolling a 2})=\dfrac{1}{6}$.

flashcards.definition: Outcomes that have the same probability.
flashcards.example: Heads and tails on a fair coin are equally likely, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

flashcards.definition: The opposite of an event; the event does not happen.
Events that cannot happen at the same time.
flashcards.example: Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on one die roll are mutually exclusive.

flashcards.definition: One event does not affect the probability of the other.
flashcards.example: Rolling a die and flipping a coin are independent; the die result does not change $P(\text{heads})$.

questions.stem: Which value represents an impossible event?
questions.explanation: A probability of 0 means the event can never happen. A probability of 1 means it is certain.

questions.stem: A bag contains 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What is $P(\text{red})$?
questions.explanation: There are 3 red marbles out of 10 marbles in total, so $P(\text{red})=\dfrac{3}{10}$.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled once. What is $P(\text{even})$?
questions.explanation: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so there are 3 favourable outcomes out of 6. $P=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: A letter is chosen at random from the word MATH. What is $P(\text{M})$?
questions.explanation: There are 4 letters in MATH and one M, so the probability is $\dfrac{1}{4}$.

questions.stem: Two fair coins are flipped. How many possible outcomes are in the sample space?
questions.explanation: The sample space is HH, HT, TH, TT, which gives 4 equally likely outcomes.

questions.stem: Two fair coins are flipped. What is $P(\text{at least one tail})$?
questions.explanation: HT, TH and TT all contain at least one tail. That is 3 out of 4 outcomes, so $P=\dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.stem: A spinner has four equal sections: red, blue, green and yellow. What is $P(\text{red or yellow})$?
questions.explanation: Two of the four equal sections are red or yellow, so $P=\dfrac{2}{4}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: Which of these values CANNOT be a probability?
questions.explanation: Probabilities must be between 0 and 1 inclusive. 1.2 is greater than 1, so it cannot be a probability.

questions.stem: A spinner is spun 50 times and lands on red 18 times. What is the experimental probability of red?
questions.explanation: Experimental probability is successes divided by trials: $\dfrac{18}{50}=\dfrac{9}{25}$.

questions.stem: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is $P(\text{total }=7)$?
questions.explanation: There are 36 equally likely outcomes and 6 ways to score 7, so $P=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac{1}{6}$.

questions.stem: A class has 12 girls and 18 boys. One student is chosen at random. What is $P(\text{girl})$?
A spinner is divided into 5 equal sections: red, red, blue, green and yellow. What is $P(\text{red})$?
questions.explanation: There are 5 equal sections and 2 are red, so $P(\text{red})=\dfrac{2}{5}$.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled 120 times. How many sixes would you expect?
questions.explanation: The theoretical probability of a six is $\dfrac{1}{6}$. Expected number $=120\times\dfrac{1}{6}=20$.

questions.stem: Tom has a bag of 20 sweets: 8 strawberry, 7 lemon and 5 orange. He picks one sweet at random. What is $P(\text{not orange})$?
questions.explanation: There are 5 orange sweets, so 15 are not orange. $P(\text{not orange})=\dfrac{15}{20}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
